summaries.summary: Speech-to-Text translation is important in scenarios such as emergency calls and online courses, with cascaded methods dominant and end-to-end methods offering lower latency and theoretically reducing error propagation.

Comprehensive experiments on the IWSLT18 speech translation benchmark show effectiveness of each component, with improvements of 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU scores for subword-level and character-level decoding.

End-to-end speech translation is formulated as learning from speech features, transcriptions, translations, ASR, MT, and ST datasets to generate target translations without intermediate transcriptions.
Following BIBREF9 inaguma2018speech, the model uses a CNN-BiLSTM architecture where input features are passed into two convolutional layers followed by max-pooling.
Experiments are conducted on the IWSLT18 speech translation task, and competitive baselines are reproduced based on ESPnet BIBREF12 for fair comparison.
The organizer provides ST-TED from TED talks, containing 272 hours of English speech with 171k segments, with 2k dev segments and tst2010, tst2013, tst2014, tst2015 as test sets.
Aside from ST-TED, TED-LIUM2 corpus BIBREF13 provides speech recognition data containing 207 hours of English speech and 93k transcript sentences.
ST-TED and WIT3 provide in-domain MT data with 130k and 200k sentence pairs, while WMT2018 provides 41M out-of-domain sentence pairs.

Data preprocessing uses 25 ms windows, 10 ms steps, 80-channel log-Mel filter bank and 3-dimensional pitch features from Kaldi BIBREF14, yielding 83-dimensional inputs, with normalization, filtering, lowercasing, punctuation removal, speed factors 0.9 and 1.1, length filtering, length-ratio filtering, Moses tokenization, and lower-case English and German words.
Subword experiments use English and German vocabularies generated by sentencepiece BIBREF15 with 5k tokens, while character experiments represent both languages at character level.
Evaluation segments audio with LIUM SpkDiarization tool BIBREF16 and MWER segmentation with RWTH toolkit BIBREF17, using lowercase BLEU as evaluation metric.
The method is compared with the following baselines.
The vanilla ST BIBREF9 baseline has only a speech encoder and a decoder and is trained from scratch on the ST-TED corpus.
All baselines and TCEN are implemented based on ESPnet BIBREF12 with RNN size d=1024, dropout of 0.3, Adadelta, initial learning rate of 1.0, and a maximum of 10 epochs.
Testing selects the model with best speech translation accuracy on dev set, and inference uses beam size of 10 with length normalization weight of 0.2.

Table TABREF29 shows the method outperforms the strong `many-to-many+pretrain' baseline by 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU scores, with pre-training more effective than multi-task learning, degradation in `triangle+pretrain', and char-level models outperforming subword-level models.

The end-to-end model is compared with cascaded systems built from ASR and MT models, including cascaded+re-seg, and outperforms the simple cascaded model over 2 BLEU scores while achieving comparable performance with re-segmentation.

Early speech translation works use pipeline methods with ASR output lattices fed into MT systems, using HMM BIBREF21, DenseNet BIBREF22, TDNN BIBREF23, RNN with attention BIBREF19, Transformer BIBREF10, and noise simulation for robustness.

Recent end-to-end works avoid error propagation and high latency by translating acoustic speech directly, using pre-training, multi-task learning, curriculum learning, attention-passing, knowledge distillation, transcriptions, and pre-trained MT and TTS synthesis models.
Because large-scale ST data is hard to obtain, ASR and MT pre-training initializes ST models, but this creates a huge pre-training and fine-tuning gap.
Subnet Waste occurs because the ST system reuses only the ASR encoder and MT decoder, discarding pre-trained subnets such as the MT encoder.
Role Mismatch arises because the speech encoder is purely acoustic in pre-training but must additionally extract semantic and linguistic features in fine-tuning.
Previous work trains separate attention modules for ASR, MT and ST, so the ST attention module does not benefit from pre-training.
TCEN reuses all pre-trained subnets, keeps subnet roles consistent, pre-trains attention, and uses a CTC-trained ASR encoder, MT-pre-trained text encoder and decoder, and multi-task learning.
TCEN concatenates an ASR encoder and MT encoder without an ASR decoder, uses tandem encoders for role consistency, and reuses the pre-trained MT attention module in ST.
TCEN achieves semantic consistency by sharing the CTC projection matrix with word embeddings and length consistency by lengthening MT source sentences with repetitions and blank tokens.
The contributions explain insufficient pre-training knowledge use in previous ST models, propose a new ST model, and empirically evaluate it on a large-scale public dataset.
Multi-task learning and pre-training leverage large scale ASR and MT data through one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many strategies for ST.
A many-to-many multi-task model has two encoders, two decoders, and three task-specific attentions, and is jointly trained on ASR, MT, and ST tasks.

Because $\mathcal {A}$ and $\mathcal {M}$ are usually much larger than $\mathcal {S}$, common pre-training and multi-task fine-tuning suffers from subnet waste, role mismatch, and non-pre-trained attention.
This section introduces the TCEN architecture, its pre-training and fine-tuning strategy, and solutions for semantic and length inconsistency caused by multi-task learning.

TCEN includes a speech encoder $enc_s$, a text encoder $enc_t$, and a decoder $dec$ with attention $att$, disentangling acoustic and linguistic feature extraction while using every pre-trained module.
Following BIBREF9 inaguma2018speech, TCEN uses CNN-BiLSTM, with input features $\mathbf {x}$ of length $T_x$ passed through two convolutional layers and max-pooling.
Max-pooling downsamples the sequence length by a total factor of four, then five bidirectional $d$-dimensional LSTM layers process the down-sampled feature sequence.
The speech encoder output is $\mathbf {h^s}=(h^s_1, \cdots , h^s_{\frac{T_x}{4}})$, where $h_i^s \in \mathbb {R}^d$.
The text encoder $enc_t$ has two bidirectional LSTM layers, consumes $\mathbf {h}^s$ in ST and $\mathbf {e^s}$ in MT, and faces semantic and length inconsistency.
The decoder has two unidirectional LSTM layers with additive attention $att$ and predicts target sequence $\mathbf {y^{t}}$ by estimating $P(\mathbf {y^{t}}|\mathbf {x})$.
Here, $z_k$ is the decoder RNN hidden state at $k$ step and $c_k$ is a time-dependent context vector computed by attention $att$.
Training splits into pre-training, where $enc_s$ uses CTC on $\mathcal {A}$ and $enc_t$ and $dec$ use $\mathcal {M}$, and fine-tuning on ASR, MT, and ST.
To sufficiently utilize large dataset $\mathcal {A}$ and $\mathcal {M}$, the model is pre-trained on CTC-based ASR task and MT task.
For ASR, CTC BIBREF8 loss trains the speech encoder to remove the decoder requirement and enable $enc_s$ to generate subword representation.
Given input $\mathbf {x}$, $enc_s$ emits $\mathbf {h^s}$, and a softmax classification layer predicts CTC path $\mathbf {\pi }$ with labels from $V_{src} \cup$ {`-'}.
$W_{ctc} \in \mathbb {R}^{d \times (|V_{src}|+1)}$ is the classification layer weight matrix and $T$ is the total length of encoder RNN.
A legal CTC path $\mathbf {\pi }$ varies source transcription $\mathbf {y}^s$ with blank tokens and repetitions, and CTC maximizes the probability of $\mathbf {y}^s$ by summing legal paths.
$\Phi _T(y)$ is the set of all legal CTC paths for sequence $\mathbf {y}$ with length $T$, and the loss is computed using the forward-backward algorithm.
For MT, cross-entropy loss trains with $\mathbf {y^s}$ converted to $\mathbf {e^s}$ through $W_{E^s}$, then $enc_t$ consumes $\mathbf {e^s}$ and passes $\mathbf {h^t}$ to the decoder.
In fine-tune stage, the model is jointly updated on ASR, MT, and ST tasks, with ASR and MT following the pre-training process.
For ST, $enc_s$ reads $\mathbf {x}$ and generates $\mathbf {h^s}$, $enc_t$ learns high-level linguistic knowledge into $\mathbf {h^t}$, and $dec$ predicts the target sentence.
Following BIBREF11 luong2015multi, each task has training ratio $\alpha _i$, and task $i$ is selected with probability $\frac{\alpha _i}{\sum _{j}\alpha _{j}}$.
Connecting two encoders for ST keeps role consistency but causes semantic inconsistency between $\mathbf {e^s}$ and $\mathbf {h^s}$ and length inconsistency between their lengths.
The countermeasures share weights between the CTC classification layer and source-end word embedding layer and feed text encoder source sentences in CTC path format generated by a seq2seq model.
During multi-task training, $enc_t$ receives $\mathbf {e}^s$ in MT and $\mathbf {h^s}$ in ST, which may belong to different latent spaces and limit individual task performance.
To bridge the space gap, $W_{ctc}$ is shared with $W_{E^s}$ so $W_{ctc} = W_{E^s}$, and CTC path probability $p(\pi _t=w_i|\mathbf {x})$ uses $h_t^s$ and the $i$-th vector in $W_{E^s}$.
The loss function closes the distance between $h^s_t$ and the golden embedding vector, encouraging $\mathbf {h}^s$ to have the same distribution with $\mathbf {e}^s$.
Length inconsistency arises because $\mathbf {h^s}$ length is proportional to input frame $\mathbf {x}$ and much longer than $\mathbf {e^s}$, addressed by an RNN-based seq2seq model and denoising MT.

A CTC ASR model trained on $\mathcal {A} = \lbrace (\mathbf {x}_i, \mathbf {y}^s_i)\rbrace _{i=0}^{I}$ generates CTC-path $\mathbf {\pi }_i$, and reversible $S(\cdot )$ converts $\mathbf {\pi }$ to $\mathbf {u}$ and $\mathbf {l}$.
Dataset $\mathcal {P}$ trains a seq2seq model to produce noisy MT dataset $\mathcal {M}^{\prime }$, and about $30\%$ pairs are sampled from $\mathcal {M}^{\prime }$ after tuning hyper-parameter $k$.
Three pre-training baselines initialize the ST encoder, decoder, or both, with ASR trained on ST-TED and TED-LIUM2 and MT trained on WMT data then in-domain data.

Three multi-task baselines use one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many settings, with $\alpha _{st}=0.75$ and $\alpha _{asr}=0.25$ or $\alpha _{mt}=0.25$, or $\alpha _{st}=0.6, \alpha _{asr}=0.2$ and $\alpha _{mt}=0.2$.

Many-to-many+pre-training derives encoders and decoders from pre-trained ASR and MT models, while Triangle+pre-train uses BIBREF18 DBLP:conf/naacl/AnastasopoulosC18's triangle multi-task strategy with initialized speech encoder and ASR decoder.
All baselines and TCEN use ESPnet BIBREF12, RNN size $d=1024$, dropout of 0.3, Adadelta with initial learning rate of 1.0, and a maximum of 10 epochs.
For TCEN pre-training, $\alpha _{asr}=0.2$ and $\alpha _{mt}=0.8$; for fine-tune, $\alpha _{st}=0.6, \alpha _{asr}=0.2$ and $\alpha _{mt}=0.2$, same as the `many-to-many' baseline.

Ablation study on subword-level experiments shows `-MT noise', `-weight sharing', and `-pretrain' degrade performance, with `-weight sharing' worse and `-pretrain' causing a dramatic BLEU score decrease.
TCEN achieves a higher final result from a better fine-tuning start-point, outperforming `many-to-many+pretrain' by about five points in subword accuracy throughout fine-tuning.
The paper investigates end-to-end ST, explains the pre-training and fine-tuning gap, proposes reusing every sub-net with consistent roles, and reports significant baseline improvements.
